sources.note: Boraana, not Waata: 'In Boraana Oromo short vowel noun endings have penultimate or ultimate stress... depending on whether they are feminine (penultimate) or masculine (ultimate).' Tertiary; not used for Waata.

sources.note: Only three Waata literacy/health booklets (Titisa; D'ukuh maleeriah yed'anih waamanu; Maleeriah; trial editions 2013). No phonology or orthography statement listed. BTL Kenya's Waata project page mentions an orthography completed January 2013 but posts no document.

sources.citation: Hoskins, Dale R. 2011. Phonology of the Orma Language. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-007. Dallas: SIL International. 39 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Orma phonology, not Waata. Section 8.3 'Tone in other Oromo languages' (printed p. 35, PDF p. 36) quotes Heine 1981: 23 second-hand: tone 'does not seem to have any distinctive function in Waata'. Fn. 20: Tana River Waata and Orma consider their languages identical. Nothing on Waata stress placement; for Orma it reports the BTL 2005 view that 'Tone functions independently of stress' and that Oromo languages may be pitch-accent.

sources.citation: Appleyard, David L. 1991. The role of tone in some Cushitic languages. York Papers in Linguistics 15: 5-32 (ERIC ED338062).
sources.note: Mentions Waata only for subject-case suffix shapes (-ni; -t(i)n); fn. 14: 'Stroomer inconsistently speaks of stress in his analysis of the three southern dialects, Booran, Orma, and Waata.' No Waata stress rule given.

sources.citation: Owens, Jonathan. 1985. A grammar of Harar Oromo (Northeastern Ethiopia). Hamburg: Buske. Rosetta Project excerpt (ch. 1-2).
sources.note: Harar Oromo; one aside on Waata: 'Unlike other Oromo dialects (eg. Booran, Waata) final short /a/ is generally maintained.' Nothing on Waata stress.
